answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: It is the last thought in “Bat It Out!” ↗, an article bylined By George Herman (‘Babe’) Ruth in The Rotarian of July 1940, starting on p. 12. We read the scan: Ruth builds to it through Henry Ford and a runner sprinting out a hopeless ground ball, then ends — “Any way you look at it, it’s a great game — baseball or life.”

source.heading: The last line of "Bat It Out!"

docMeta.dd: The Rotarian, July 1940 (Vol. 57, Iss. 1), from p. 12
An as-told-to piece — the magazine sent the writer Doron K. Antrim to Ruth

source.excerpt: A good player never stops until he’s actually out, running as hard for first base on the almost-certain-to-be-caught fly or grounder as he would if he were sprinting the 100-yard dash. If Henry Ford hadn’t kept going in the early days despite ridicule, we would never have seen the Ford car. It’s been much the same with almost every great man you could name. He kept plugging when everybody said his chances of making first base were nil. You just can’t beat the person who never gives up.
trail: We read the primary. The full text of The Rotarian, July 1940 ↗ contains the sentence exactly once, at the end of an article headed “Bat It Out!” and bylined By George Herman (‘Babe’) Ruth. The issue’s own running heads date it July 1940 and the article begins on p. 12 — matching Wikiquote’s citation ↗ of pp. 12–14.

The same scan shows how the piece was made: the magazine’s editors “went to Doron K. Antrim, who, in turn, went to ‘Babe’ Ruth”, and Ruth said he would “pretend he were talking to boys”. So the byline is his and the words are his as taken down by a professional writer — the normal arrangement for Ruth’s published prose.

A bonus from reading the whole article: Ruth restates the team-play maxim from his 1928 book ↗ here in fresh words — “You may have the greatest bunch of individual stars in the world, but if they don’t play together the club won’t be worth a dime.” Twelve years apart, same point.
source.excerptNote: Quoted from the Internet Archive’s scan of the July 1940 issue. The article closes a few lines later, with Ruth wishing his readers “a home-run record in life’s game”.

author.name: Babe Ruth
author.heading: About Babe Ruth
author.bio: George Herman “Babe” Ruth played 22 seasons in Major League Baseball, from 1914 to 1935, and remade the sport around the home run. He retired in 1935 and spent his last years hoping for a managing job that never arrived. He remained a prolific by-lined writer for magazines and newspapers, almost always working with a professional writer at his elbow.

misattribution.heading: The version that circulates
misattribution.intro: Ruth is the right author. The sentence you have most likely seen is not quite the one he published.

items.why: A smoother form — “It’s hard to beat a person who never gives up” — travels widely, and Wikiquote’s own page ↗ uses that version as a photo caption while its sourced entry gives the published wording. The 1940 original, which we read, is “You just can’t beat the person who never gives up.”

misattribution.truthLine: Both say the same thing, and only one of them is in the magazine ↗. If you are citing it, cite the published sentence.

context.heading: Ruth in 1940
lead: Ruth had been out of baseball for five years when this appeared, and he badly wanted a job managing that never came. So the piece is a retired man addressing boys about persistence, which gives the closing line a weight it would not have had from a player mid-career.

It is also a period document in a way that is easy to miss: it ran in a service-club magazine in July 1940, alongside articles about wartime rationing in Britain, and its argument is that the habits of the ball field carry over into a job.
context.pull: Any way you look at it, it’s a great game — baseball or life.

Wikiquote’s sourced section attributes this wording to "Bat It Out!" by George Herman ('Babe') Ruth in The Rotarian, pp. 12-14, and separately illustrates its page with the variant "It's hard to beat a person who never gives up."
